title: Wagon wheels and aliasing
teaches: Sampling, Nyquist and why a recording played faster turns into a chipmunk

blocks.text: **The sound.** Here is a short sung "wow", stored as numbers, played on three keys an octave apart. On the low key it plays as it was sung. An octave up it plays twice as fast, so it is higher and shorter, and the voice turns into a cartoon. The second sound is the same thing cut short and deliberately made coarse, a sound from 1980s hip hop. You'll make that one at the end.

blocks.caption: A sung “wow” played an octave apart, then cut and crushed

blocks.text: An engine that plays a stored sound is a **sampler**, and the stored sound is a **sample**. It doesn't make a wave; it plays one back. To play a note higher, the simplest sampler plays the recording faster, as a tape machine does when it is sped up. Everything in it rises together: the pitch, the vowels of the voice and the speed. That's the chipmunk.[^chipmunk]

A sample is a list of numbers, each one the pressure of the sound at one instant: the height of the wave, measured many thousands of times a second. The number of measurements a second is the **sample rate**. A CD uses 44,100. Playing back means turning the numbers back into pressure, one after another, at the same rate.

On the sample engine, **Wave** is where in the sample a note starts, and **Timbre** is how much of it plays from there. Start late, and the note skips the breath at the beginning and goes straight into the vowel. Play only a little, and you have a short slice of it. Cutting samples into slices like this is the basis of a great deal of music.

blocks.caption: The sample, played from the start. Start it later.

blocks.text: **The mystery.** In old Westerns a wagon rolls forward, faster and faster, and its spoked wheels seem to slow down, stop and turn backwards. The wheels are fine. The film is the trouble: it takes 24 pictures a second, and when a spoke moves nearly the gap to the next spoke between two pictures, it looks as if it moved a little backwards instead.

Sampling a sound does the same thing to a tone. If the tone rises and falls more than once between two samples, the samples can't tell, and they trace out a slower tone that was never there. A sample rate can only hold tones below half itself. That limit is called the **Nyquist frequency**, after Harry Nyquist of Bell Labs. A tone above it doesn't disappear. It comes back down, folded under the limit, as a false tone called an **alias**.

blocks.caption: A tone sampled 4,000 times a second. The dots are the samples; the dashed line is what comes back out. Play it.
blocks.task: Turn the tone to 3 kHz or more

blocks.text: As the tone rises past half the sample rate, what you hear goes down. That's the backwards wagon wheel for the ear. Recorders avoid it with a filter that removes everything above the limit before sampling, and the 44,100 of a CD puts the limit just above the highest pitch most people can hear.

Early samplers had little memory, so they sampled slowly and stored each number coarsely. The Fairlight CMI of 1979 and the Emulator of 1981 cost as much as a house, and their samples had a grainy edge. A drum machine of 1987, the E-mu SP-1200, sampled at about 26,000 a second in 12-bit numbers, and its gritty drums became part of the sound of hip hop. When memory grew cheap, producers kept the grit on purpose.

On this engine, **Shape** lowers the sample rate after the sample, with no filter in front, so the aliases come through. A little adds a fizzy edge, and a lot turns the voice into a metallic, ringing version of itself. The false tones don't follow the note's pitch the way harmonics do, so a crushed note sounds slightly out of tune with itself. That's the sound.
Now make the opening's second sound from a plain saw. You need the engine, where the slice starts, how much of it plays, and how coarse it is.

blocks.caption: A plain saw. Make the cut and crushed sample.
blocks.task: Make the cut and crushed sample

blocks.text: A sample doesn't have to be played as a note at all. The next lesson cuts it into crumbs a few hundredths of a second long and scatters them, which is granular synthesis.

blocks.caption: Four questions on samples
blocks.task: Choose the best answer to each

items.ask: A simple sampler plays a note an octave up. What happens to the sample?
choices: It plays twice as fast: higher and shorter
It plays at the same speed, higher
items.why: Like a tape sped up, everything rises and speeds up together.

choices: How many measurements of the wave are taken each second
How many samples the synth holds
items.why: A CD takes 44,100 measurements a second.

items.ask: What happens to a tone above half the sample rate?
choices: It comes back as a lower false tone, an alias
items.why: The samples trace a slower tone: the backwards wagon wheel for the ear.

items.ask: Why did producers keep coarse sampling once memory was cheap?
choices: They liked the gritty sound it gives
items.why: The grit of early samplers became part of the music's sound.

summary: **A sampler plays back a stored sound**, the sample, instead of making a wave.
**Played higher, a sample plays faster**: pitch, vowels and speed all rise together, like a sped-up tape.
**A sample is a list of measurements**; how many a second is the sample rate (44,100 on a CD).
**Start point and length cut a slice** out of the sample.
**A sample rate holds only tones below half itself**, the Nyquist frequency.
**Tones above it fold back down as aliases**, as film makes wagon wheels turn backwards.
**Coarse sampling on purpose** gives the grit of early samplers.

chipmunk.title: The Chipmunks
chipmunk.text: In 1958 Ross Bagdasarian recorded his own voice singing slowly, with the tape running at half speed, and played it back at full speed. It came out an octave higher and twice as fast, and became Alvin and the Chipmunks. Samplers today can change pitch without changing speed, by cutting the sound into tiny pieces and overlapping them, which is the grains of the next lesson.
